content: 1. The formulation must be protected from excessive temperature and moisture to maintain its integrity and effectiveness. 2. The formulation is expected to include a dye or pigment that permanently colors the seed after treatment. Red is the recommended color for this purpose. 3. For specific applications, the dye or pigment can be added at a later stage if necessary. 4. In some countries, there may be legal requirements mandating the use of a specific color for treated seeds. 5. The same color used for seed treatment must not be used for denaturing seeds intended for livestock feed, to avoid confusion or misuse. 6. Methods of analysis must comply with CIPAC, AOAC, or equivalent standards. If the methods have not yet been published, full details, including appropriate method validation data, must be submitted to FAO/WHO by the proposer. 7. If both g/kg and g/L at 20°C are required by the buyer, in case of dispute, the analytical results should be calculated as g/kg. 8. Only relevant impurities should be included in the specification clause, and the title should reflect the name of the relevant impurity. Methods of analysis must be peer-validated. 9. The method to be used for analysis must be explicitly stated. If multiple methods are available, a referee method must be selected. 10. Micro-emulsions are mixtures of water, water-insoluble, and water-soluble components that form a visually homogeneous, transparent liquid. Active ingredients may be present in the aqueous phase, the non-aqueous phase, or both. 11. Micro-emulsions disperse into water to form either conventional emulsions or dilute micro-emulsions. They are thermodynamically stable, unlike other conventional dispersion formulations, but are often stable only within limited temperature ranges. 12. Particular attention must be given to storage instructions for micro-emulsions, as they may form emulsions or dilute micro-emulsions upon dilution in water. 13. Micro-emulsions should be treated similarly to emulsifiable concentrate (EC) formulations, with modifications to account for potential issues related to storage and use at extreme temperatures. 14. Suspension concentrates (SC) are stable suspensions of active ingredients in an aqueous continuous phase, intended for dilution with water before use. 15. The performance characteristics of SCs are best described by parameters such as pourability, water dispersibility, suspensibility, wet sieve analysis, and persistent foam tests. 16. Particle size range and viscosity are excluded from SC specifications due to the lack of simple, internationally accepted methods for their determination. Instead, parameters like wet sieve analysis, suspensibility, and pourability adequately describe these properties. 17. Before sampling a commercial container to verify formulation quality, inspect it carefully to ensure no phase separation has occurred. If the formulation has been exposed to temperature extremes, gentle agitation may be required to restore it to a transparent, homogeneous liquid. 18. Suspension concentrates often develop a concentration gradient from top to bottom during storage, which may result in a clear liquid on top and sediment at the bottom. Homogenize the formulation before sampling, following the manufacturer’s instructions or by gently shaking the container. 19. Large containers must be opened and stirred adequately to ensure homogeneity. After homogenization, the container should not contain a sticky layer of non-dispersed material at the bottom. 20. All physical and chemical tests must be conducted on a sample taken after the recommended homogenization procedure. 21. The influence of seed treatment on germination is critical but is not included as a specification clause due to the lack of a universally applicable test method for all seed types. 22. Users must strictly follow the manufacturer’s recommendations for applying the formulation and should not treat seeds for which the effect on germination is unknown. 23. Treated seeds should be stored in suitable containers and protected from excessive temperature and moisture. 24. The manufacturer must declare the minimum percentage of the active ingredient remaining on the seeds after treatment for a representative seed type. 25. The formulation must be homogeneous after gentle stirring or shaking and suitable for further dilution with water if necessary. 26. The active ingredient must comply with an identity test and, if necessary, at least one additional test to confirm its identity. 27. Chemical assay is the most reliable method to measure the mass of active ingredients still in suspension. In case of dispute, the chemical method shall be the referee method. 28. The mass of the sample used in tests should correspond to the highest recommended rate of use by the supplier. Tests should be conducted in CIPAC standard water D. 29. In certain circumstances, phase separation may occur at high or low temperatures. The formulation is acceptable if recovery to a single phase is as rapid as thermal equilibrium with ambient or use temperatures. 30. Treated seeds must be permanently colored to distinguish them from untreated seeds. Red is recommended, but specific legal requirements for color may apply in some countries.
